colony: a land ruled by another country
independence: being free to rule yourself
generation: all the people born around the same time
protest: showing publicly that you think something is wrong
republic: a country with no king or queen, led by chosen leaders
government: the group of people who run a country
nation: a country and its people

chapters.title: Life Under the Flag That Was Not Theirs

pages.text: When the Scramble ended, most of Africa woke each morning under a flag chosen by strangers. In the land now called Nigeria, the British made the rules, collected the taxes and named the officials. Africans did the work of their own country, but the top jobs, and the biggest profits, went to men from far away.

image.note: 1920s Lagos street: African clerks, market women, a British official on a veranda above them

pages.text: It was not that Africans were content. A person can obey a rule and still know it is unjust. All across the continent, in markets, in mission schools and in quiet family talk, the same question was being asked. Why should our own land be ruled by people who are not from here?

image.note: Family talking low by lamplight; an older woman speaking, children listening

pages.text: The colonial rulers had made one mistake that would cost them dearly. To run the colonies, they needed clerks, teachers and lawyers, so they built schools. In those schools, a new generation of Africans learned to read, to argue and to organise. The rulers had, without meaning to, trained the very people who would one day ask them to leave.

image.note: A mission-school classroom, sharp-eyed African students at desks, a map of the world on the wall

chapters.title: The Ones Who Went Away and Came Back

pages.text: Some of those bright students travelled overseas to study, to London, to America. There, something surprising happened. They saw that the rulers of the empire were ordinary people, no cleverer than themselves. And they met other Africans and Caribbeans who all asked the same question. Why not us? Why not free?

image.note: African students on a cold London street in coats, talking intently, breath misting

pages.text: They came home changed, and they carried names that Nigeria would never forget. Nnamdi Azikiwe, who had studied in America, returned and started newspapers that spoke plainly about freedom. Obafemi Awolowo and Ahmadu Bello built movements in the west and the north. They were not soldiers. Their weapons were words, plans and patience.

image.note: Three dignified vignette portraits: a newspaperman at a printing press, a lawyer with papers, a northern leader in flowing robes

pages.text: These leaders did not always agree with one another. Nigeria was vast, with many peoples, and each region had its own hopes and fears. But on one thing they agreed completely. The time of being ruled by others must come to an end.

image.note: A meeting table, three leaders leaning in over a map of Nigeria, serious and united on the one point

pages.text: After the great world war of the 1940s, everything shifted. Africans had fought and died in that war for Britain, and they came home asking a fair question. We fought for your freedom. Where is ours? Across Africa, the demand for independence grew from a whisper into a roar.

image.note: African ex-servicemen in uniform marching home, medals on their chests, faces set

pages.text: In 1957, the country then called the Gold Coast became free and chose a new name, Ghana. It was the first colony south of the Sahara to win its independence, and its success rang across the continent like a bell. If Ghana could be free, so could Nigeria. So could everyone.

image.note: Jubilant Accra crowd, a new flag rising, drums; pure celebration

pages.text: Even a British leader admitted it. Standing in Africa, the Prime Minister of Britain said that a wind of change was blowing across the continent, and that it could not be stopped. He was right. One after another, the colonies were becoming nations again.

image.note: A formal 1960 podium scene, an African audience listening; flags streaming in wind

pages.text: How do you win a country back without an army? The Nigerian leaders showed how. They wrote in newspapers so ordinary people could read the truth. They formed political parties so millions of voices became one voice. They travelled to London, again and again, to argue Nigeria's case across a table.

image.note: Split image: a newspaper being read on a bus; a packed party rally; suited delegates in a London conference room

pages.text: Ordinary people mattered most of all. Market women in the towns, who controlled the trade, refused unfair taxes and organised protests that the rulers could not ignore. Workers went on strike. The struggle for freedom was not only for great men in fine clothes. It belonged to everybody.

image.note: A crowd of determined market women, wrappers and headties, standing firm together in a marketplace

pages.text: Step by step, it worked. The British agreed to let Nigerians vote and run more of their own affairs. Each election, each new agreement, moved the country closer to the day it wanted. Freedom was not given in one gift. It was won piece by piece, by patient, stubborn people.

image.note: Nigerians queuing to vote, a ballot box, pride on their faces

chapters.title: The Day the Flag Came Down

pages.text: At last the day was set. The first of October, 1960. On the night before, a great crowd gathered in Lagos and waited as the clock crawled towards midnight. Sixty years of foreign rule were ending, and everyone there wanted to see it with their own eyes.

image.note: Huge night crowd in a Lagos stadium, floodlights, faces turned upward, breath held

pages.text: At the stroke of midnight, the British flag was lowered for the last time. In its place rose a new flag, green and white and green, chosen by Nigerians for their own land. The green was for the fields and forests, the white for peace. As it climbed the pole, the whole crowd roared.

image.note: The green-white-green flag rising against a night sky; the crowd's arms lifted, mouths open in a cheer

pages.text: Nigeria was free. It was its own country, with its own government, choosing its own path for the first time in living memory. Grown men wept. Strangers embraced. Somewhere a child asked what it all meant, and was told, tonight, this country belongs to us.

image.note: An elder holding a small child up to see the flag, both lit by stadium light, tears and joy

pages.text: But freedom, they soon learned, was not the end of the story. It was the start of a much harder one. Winning a country is one task. Running it well is another, and it never truly finishes.

image.note: The morning after: an empty stadium at dawn, one worker sweeping, the new flag still flying

pages.text: Nigeria had been stitched together by the British from many peoples who had not chosen to be one nation. Now those peoples had to learn to trust one another and share power fairly. It was not easy, and at times it went badly wrong. Building a nation, it turned out, was slower than winning one.

image.note: A map of Nigeria's regions, hands from different directions reaching to hold it together

pages.text: Yet the great thing had been done. Whatever troubles came after, they were now Nigeria's own troubles to solve, in Nigeria's own way. No one across the sea would decide any longer. And the same story was unfolding all over the continent, as colony after colony took back its name and its future.

image.note: A wall of new African flags of the 1960s, bright and varied, filling the frame

pages.text: So when you see the green-white-green flag flying over your school, remember that it did not always fly there, and that it was not a gift. People imagined it, argued for it, and worked for years so that you would grow up free in your own country. The flag is a promise, and now the promise is yours to keep.

image.note: A present-day Nigerian child looking up at the flag over a modern school, morning light, hopeful
